extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent agents/practitioners, and advisors on patent validity (UK-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining novelty, prior publication/public user issues, and the required amount of invention (inventive step/utility) to support a patent, with statutory and case-law examples. Focused on practical advising and litigation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-publication must enable practical use (enablement test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge of an invention to avoid a patent must be a knowledge equal to that required to be given by a patent, viz. such a knowledge as will enable the public to perceive the very discovery, and to carry the invention into practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent generality or broad propositions do not necessarily prejudice a later limited, accurate statement. The prior disclosure must be sufficient to enable a workman to make and use the invention; mere mention or partial description that does not enable practical reproduction will not be treated as anticipatory publication. (Illustrated by cases where provisional or incomplete descriptions did not vitiate later patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair-reading test for prior specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: whether the prior specification, fairly read by a person conversant with such matters, would give a reasonably clear description of the later invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a skilled-person 'fair reading' of the earlier specification: would it show a machine (or other apparatus) that would effect what the later invention effects? Case law cited: Otto v. Linford and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of language is not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if there is identity of language in two specifications, one cannot conclude they describe the same external object unless terms of art in each have precisely the same signification at the respective dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware verbatim overlap: differences in the meaning of technical terms over time or contextual differences may mean the prior text does not in law anticipate the later invention. (Quoted from Lord Westbury in Betts v. Menzies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete provisional specifications may not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification containing an incomplete description that is omitted from the complete specification is not a prior publication if the description was not sufficient to enable a workman to make the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the provisional lacks sufficient detail to enable practical construction, it will not necessarily vitiate a later complete patent. Use factual enablement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publication by inventor can destroy novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may be the true and first inventor and yet disentitle himself to a patent by prior dealings with or prior publication of the invention; one may not publish a discovery and then obtain protection against the public whom he has already informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture for sale, offering for sale, or public sale by the inventor before the patent date has been held to render the patent void (cases: Wood v. Zimmer, Germ Milling Co. v. Robinson). Mere private possession does not necessarily forfeit rights, but delay and public commercial activity are dangerous. Depositing a machine in a room open to the public for testing may be acceptable for a 'reasonable time' (Bentley v. Fleming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential communications are not publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating the discovery to a few persons under an obligation of confidence does not constitute publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure is made under injunctions of secrecy / explicit confidentiality and kept secret, it will not be treated as giving the invention to the public (example: Galloway / Morgan facts in Morgan v. Setcard). Even if construction occurs at a third party's works under secrecy, that can remain private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use exception (necessary disclosure during testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure during the course of experiments made by the patentee for testing or improving the invention (unavoidable and no more than necessary) will not take away the inventor's right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples sent out or testing in presence of others may be treated as experiments if done to perfect the invention and not as public giving. However, if the inventor derives profit from use and the public has free access (Re Adamson) the use may become public user. Distinguish purely experimental/necessary disclosures from commercial/public exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication by others can anticipate (public accessibility test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of the invention by persons other than the patentee, and accessibility to persons under no obligation of secrecy, can constitute a prior publication that invalidates a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-based inquiry: were the drawings, tracings, apparatus, or explanations placed within reach of the public or persons not bound to secrecy? Examples: Saxby v. Gloucester Waggon Co. (drawings and working apparatus visible/accessible in offices and shops) and Humpherson v. Syer. L.J. Fry's practical test: was it the fair conclusion some English people, under no obligation to secrecy, knew of the invention at the date of the patent?

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exhibition safe only if statutory conditions met
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibiting an invention at a certified industrial or international exhibition does not prejudice the right to apply for a patent provided statutory procedures are followed (section 39 of the Act of 1883, Rule 15 Patents Rules 1890, and section 3 of Act 1886).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions include: giving prescribed notice to the Comptroller before exhibiting; applying for a patent before or within six months from the opening of the exhibition; furnishing a brief description and drawings if necessary; paying the required stamp. Foreign exhibitions may be governed by Orders in Council relieving some conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required amount of invention (inventive_step) — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed the patentee must show not merely novelty in the sense of something not previously done, but novelty of such shape that it requires some exertion of mind that could properly be called invention; however, no precise general rule can be laid down as to the amount of ingenuity essential to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is heavily fact-dependent; courts look to precedents similar to the case at hand. In borderline cases little can be settled without judicial decision. Amount of invention may overlap with novelty analysis. Case law illustrates both ends of the spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility/Practical success can support small inventive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Where utility is great and novelty is clear, small or apparently trivial inventions may be supported; practical success and usefulness can aid what appears to be a small inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a simple method that produced large practical advantages (gas-tubes made without a mandrel; flat wick increasing illumination; flame treatment removing cotton fibres) supported patents. The difference between failure and acceptability (Edison's filament vs Swan's rod) may be decisive when the filament makes the combination successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: New combination of old parts may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of old components may be patentable if the new combination produces a useful result or effect that was not previously achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have upheld patents for novel combinations that produce practical benefits (Hayward v. Hamilton: frame + flange + moulded glass prism). The fact that parts separately were old does not preclude patentability of a novel and useful combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere mechanical equivalents or obvious applications are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere substitution, trivial alteration, or the application of well-known operations in a known manner which produces no new result or advantage will not support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where patents failed: uniting two existing parts by well-known means instead of three (Brunton v. Humphrys), fixing distances within ranges previously varied in prior art (Kay v. Marshall), and minor adjustments (piano check-action distances). If the step simply deprives the public of prior freedom to use common machinery without producing a new effect, it may be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour, expense, or accidental discovery irrelevant to patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour of thought, long experiment, or expenditure of money is not essential; if the invention is new and useful, it does not matter whether it arose by long research, a lucky thought, or accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability focuses on novelty and utility, not the amount of effort. Classic examples include inventions arising from accidental observation (water-table example) that nevertheless were held patentable because they were new and useful.
